name: tui-disk
tagline: Disks, mounts, fstab, btrfs and SMART health on one screen, with every change previewed before it runs
description:
A terminal UI for the machine's storage. Five screens over one read: the block devices with their filesystems and usage bars, the mount table crossed against `/etc/fstab`, the btrfs filesystems in full, the SMART health of every drive, and what `df` says about free space.

The mounts screen is the one that earns its keep. It shows what is mounted now next to what fstab says will be mounted next boot, and marks every row where those disagree: a filesystem mounted by hand that will vanish on reboot, an fstab entry that failed to mount and nobody noticed, and options fstab asks for that are not in effect.

Changes are previewed. Mounting and unmounting an fstab entry, starting or cancelling a btrfs scrub or balance, starting a drive self-test, and editing `/etc/fstab` — which is validated with `findmnt --verify` against the staged file *before* the dialog opens, shown as a unified diff, then installed with `install -m 644` and applied with `systemctl daemon-reload` — all go through a confirm dialog carrying the exact command line.

Reads that need root take `sudo -n` and nothing else: a machine where that prompts loses the subvolume list and the drive health, keeps everything else, and says which.

Run `tui-disk --demo` to drive a sample machine: an NVMe root on btrfs with three subvolumes, a spinning disk with two reallocated sectors, a USB stick mounted by hand and one fstab mismatch. Every key works, every command is built and previewed for real, and nothing touches your system.

notes.impact: lsblk has no `MOUNTPOINTS` column, so the single-valued `MOUNTPOINT` is asked for instead; a device mounted at several paths reports only the first one. lsblk fails the whole call on a column name it does not know, so this is a gate rather than a fallback

`blkid` reads /dev directly and answers an unprivileged caller with an empty body and exit 0, so the fstab editor's device picker escalates with `sudo -n` and falls back to the UUIDs lsblk already reported when it cannot

`--format json` is supported per command, not globally: `device stats` and `filesystem df` emit JSON, while `filesystem usage`, `subvolume list`, `scrub status` and `balance status` answer "output format json is unsupported for this command" through 6.19 at least, so those four are read from their text output

`subvolume list`, `qgroup show` and `balance status` refuse an unprivileged caller with "Operation not permitted"; they are retried with `sudo -n`, and a machine that cannot escalate shows those sections empty with a note saying so
no `--format json` at all, so `device stats` is read from its text output too
`smartctl --json` does not exist, and the health of every drive is reported as unknown rather than scraped out of a table meant for human eyes

reading SMART needs the raw device, so it escalates with `sudo -n`; a drive behind a USB bridge that passes no SMART through, and a virtual disk that has no firmware, both come back unknown with the reason smartctl gave

pacman.note: Add the tui-tools repository to pacman.conf first.

aur.note: The -bin package installs the released static binary.

apt.note: Add the tui-tools apt repository and its keyring first.

binary.command:
curl -fsSL https://github.com/tui-tools/tui-disk/releases/download/v{version}/tui-disk_{version}_linux_{arch}.tar.gz | tar -xz tui-disk
sudo install -m0755 tui-disk /usr/local/bin/tui-disk
binary.note: One static binary. Verify it against checksums.txt from the same release.

source.command:
git clone https://github.com/tui-tools/tui-disk
cd tui-disk && make build
sudo install -m0755 bin/tui-disk /usr/local/bin/tui-disk

security.needs_sudo: Most reads are unprivileged: lsblk, findmnt, df, `btrfs filesystem usage`, `btrfs scrub status` and `btrfs device stats` answer to any user. Four do not, and escalate with `sudo -n`, which never prompts: blkid, `btrfs subvolume list`, `btrfs qgroup show` and `btrfs balance status`, plus `smartctl -a`, which needs the raw device. A machine that cannot escalate loses those sections and keeps the rest. Every change escalates the same way: mount, umount, scrub, balance, self-test, and the `install` plus `systemctl daemon-reload` that apply an fstab edit.
